text: Measuring things relevant to upholding a pause: Assessments focused on compute allocation and RSI-relevant metrics (e.g. algorithmic efficiency, uplift measures, spend on AI agents, analysis of success rates on internal tasks) seem most relevant for creating the right kind of technical competency and relationships. One individual working in lab advocacy estimated in private conversation that there is a 20-30% chance of pacing/pausing without government involvement happening in the next 6 months. This is not high enough. I estimate the chance of pacing/pausing via the California legislature in the next 10 months (and that is not struck down within weeks by a judge) is roughly 20%. Through federal channels, I estimate 10%. These probabilities are correlated with each other, since the chances of success increase for each channel if there is a major incident, and due to other shared factors. In other words, we are not on track to succeed. My feeling is, if we develop it as quickly as we can, in the easiest way we can, we would be looking at something like a coin flip of an AI takeover. I hope the odds are much lower than that since we are not going to develop this technology in the most rapid way we can The METR report on AI R&D automation within Anthropic is substantial evidence that timelines to superintelligence are now less than 2 years, even accounting for uncertainty about takeoff modeling, the reliability of the report’s conclusions, and other types of uncertainty. Ryan Greenblatt gives a straightforward way to extrapolate METR’s findings in a tweet . He claims that “In AI 2027, [the current level of speedup by RSI] happens around March 2027.” This means that real-world AI progress on AI R&D capabilities is faster than in AI 2027, an already extremely bullish scenario. Given that in AI 2027, ASI is achieved in December 2027, this suggests superintelligence would be developed, without slowdown, around July 2027 (assuming that the original AI 2027 scenario modeled the shape of AI takeoff correctly). I think the most compelling evidence for very short timelines has been the reactions of established forecasters and researchers. In response to the METR report, the AI Futures Project released an emergency Q3.5 timelines update . Here are the all-things-considered forecasts of the team (I note that ASI is generally modeled as being reached less than a year after TED-AI absent deliberate slowdowns): These forecasts give us a very tight deadline to get a pause in place. Other reactions: As a result of the above, my current all-things-considered median date for superintelligence without a slowdown or other major intervention is around March 2028. That is around a year and a half from now. If we achieve ASI within 6-12 months, I estimate that the chance of an AI takeover is roughly 75%. (In a recent talk , Paul Christiano said it would be a coin flip.) Paired with the timelines above, unless we achieve aggressive pacing or a pause within 6-12 months, we incur something like a 1-in-4 to 1-in-3 chance of AI takeover within 12 months. This is obviously unacceptable. I believe there are three feasible paths to achieving pacing or pausing within 6-12 months, and that these should be the overwhelming priority of the AI safety community right now: Each of these should aim for pacing or pausing that gets us at the very least a 1 year slowdown in the expected date of superintelligence, such as three of the proposals in the AI Futures Project’s How to Pace the U.S. Frontier : a 10% AI R&D compute cap, a 9-month capability for AI R&D lag, or a 1-year inference-only pause. There are ongoing efforts in each of these three categories. However, there are several issues with those efforts: I’m not necessarily saying that, in some overall sense, lab advocacy, California lobbying, or federal lobbying are neglected on the margin. My claim is that lab advocacy, California lobbying, and federal lobbying with the goal of starting aggressive pacing/pausing within the next 6-12 months is greatly neglected. Any sort of pause that can last more than a year will eventually need to become a global pause. Entering a US-only pause is an important stepping stone towards entering a global pause, but I expect pressure from middle powers to be pretty important for the pause going global . I think some of the best work here amounts to improving the situational awareness of middle power governments and helping them navigate the situation with regards to the US approaching ASI. I think there are a few main categories of work that technical people should focus on: All three paths to pausing would be substantially helped by technical work focused on setting the foundations for a global pause. I think the most urgent work of this kind is third-party assessments focused on the type of investigation that would be necessary to build trust between participants of a pause. If we get practice doing lower-stakes and lower-scale versions of assessments, we can build buy-in that we could pull off a global pause. Ideally, sometime in the next few months, third parties would conduct assessments with the following properties: I talk more about the technical work that would facilitate a pause in my recent post “ We urgently need to practice before we can pause .” As I write above, I think for most people the most impactful path is to do lab advocacy, lobby the California legislature, lobby the federal government, establish evidence of risk, lay the technical foundations for a pause, or work on aligning and controlling early automated researchers. These include: I do not mean to denigrate anyone working in AI safety. I know that all of us are trying our best to preserve the future. I have tremendous respect for anyone that is earnestly doing so. But given recent evidence, many people should urgently reprioritize the work that they are doing. If labs attempt to pause they may antitrust litigation or action under statutes like the Defense Production Act to get them to continue training. If a state attempts to implement a pause through it state policy it may face dormant commerce clause, preemption, intergovernmental immunity, and first amendment arguments, as well as labs simply trying to leave the jurisdiction. Federal action might face first amendment arguments. if you think the critical time is 6-12 months, convincing the given actor to act only to loss a preliminary injunction creates a big problem for the effectiveness of the policy. Along these lines, I'm curious why you think focusing on CA is the right move? Having thought about how things might go down if a state or coalition of states tried to implement a local version of a "pause", I think they could face significant problems. That is partly what motivated this post . Many AI labs are headquartered in CA, which makes it seem like a good place to pursue legislation regulating them. But in a scenario where CA pursues an aggressive pause that labs disagree with, they could take actions to leave the jurisdiction of the state (e.g. moving HQ to another state, moving employees, refusing to offer models to citizens of the state). If the federal government agrees with labs it may also be able funnel work on AI R&D into federal contracts with the labs or otherwise place the work in the realm of national security to help the labs avoid the reach of state law. For more moderate regulation like transparency regulation I can see why CA would be a good target, but once the regulation is strong enough that labs are willing to do everything they can to avoid the regulation, including completely leaving the state, it becomes much dicier in my view. I think a more robust target would be states that have AI-capable data centers. If training is physically occurring at a data center within a state I think it would be much harder for an AI lab to try to avoid state regulation.
